# Framing a question

Cancer is interesting. That sentence is true, it isn't a question, and no
dataset anywhere can answer it. In front of you sits GSE60450: 27,179 rows of
counts, 12 columns of samples, all of it already loaded. What has to be added
to "cancer is interesting" before that file can answer it?

## What a question needs before anybody can answer it

Three things have to be written down inside it. Take one away and nothing stops
you. The file still opens and a table still comes back. You find out at the
end, holding output you have no way to read.

### It names two groups

A number out of biology almost never settles anything on its own.

"How much *Brca1* is there in mammary tissue?" gets you a number. It doesn't get
you an answer, because you can't call the number high without saying higher
than what.

So name both sides, and say how many samples sit on each. GSE60450 holds 12
samples, and most of what you can ask it comes down to cutting those 12 into
two piles. Basal against luminal is six and six. Virgin against lactating
inside the basal cells is two and two. Pile size is part of the question, and
Chapter 25 is where two-against-two starts costing you.

::: {.why}
A mouse mammary gland isn't one thing. Basal cells and luminal cells sit side
by side in it and run different genes, and the organ rebuilds itself when the
animal starts producing milk. That's why the people who made GSE60450 sorted
the cells before sequencing them: two cell types at three stages, six groups,
12 samples. "How much *Brca1* is in mammary tissue" has no answer, because the
tissue in that question is six different things.
:::

### It names the number you will compute

"Expression" is a subject. Counts per million is a measurement. The test is
whether you can name the file and the column you'd pull it out of.

Say it as a verb with a unit attached: take the mean counts per million for
*Brca1* in each group, then divide one by the other. That sentence tells you
which file to open on Saturday.

That unit is doing real work. A raw count of reads isn't expression.
It's a count out of however many reads that sample happened to get, which is
why Chapter 20 divided by library size first. Chapter 7 was the same move: an
E-value meant nothing until you knew how big the database behind it was. Name a
unit that already carries its denominator.

### It names the result that would prove you wrong

Write the sentence "I would be wrong if" before you run anything, and finish
it.

For the basal-against-luminal question it takes one line. I'd be wrong if the
mean counts per million in the two groups land within a factor of two of each
other. Two means, one division, and the run can now come back and contradict
me. A question that can't come out badly is a plan to generate a table.

Pick that factor with some care. "The six basal values never overlap the six
luminal ones" sounds stricter and therefore better, and it's the wrong bar. It
throws the question out the moment one sample lands inside the other group's
range, while the other eleven still say the groups differ.

I leave the third part off more often than the other two. It costs nothing at
all, right up to the day you have a table and no way to say whether it's the
right one.

::: {.trap}
"Which genes are highest in the lactating samples" has a comparison and a
measurement and no way to fail. Sort a column, take the top ten, and a table
comes back. Shuffle the numbers first and a table still comes back. It looks
the same: real gene names, sensible values, nothing red anywhere. You can't tell
that output apart from the one your data would give if every sample label were
wrong. Add the third part and the run gets a chance to disagree with you.
:::

Try the shape on whatever question brought you to this chapter.

::: {.check}
Write your question on one line. Underline the two groups and put the number of
samples beside each. Circle the measurement and write its unit above it. Then
finish "I would be wrong if" underneath.

Two underlines, one circle, one finished sentence. Whichever of the four you
couldn't produce is the part you're missing, and it isn't code.
:::

## Three narrowings

Here are three starting sentences, narrowed a step at a time. Every version in
between is printed, including the ones too vague to use.

### Cancer is interesting

Rewrite it as a subject and it feels like progress. "I want to work on breast
cancer genes." That isn't progress. Adding words to a topic gets you a longer
topic.

"Is *BRCA1* expressed differently in breast cancer?" has the grammar of a
question. Differently from what? Measured how? "Breast cancer" is a category,
and a category isn't a pile of samples.

Here's the version that lands. In GSE60450, do basal cells and luminal cells
differ in *Brca1* expression, measured as mean counts per million, six samples
against six? I'd be wrong if the two group means land within a factor of two.

Now the uncomfortable part, out loud: that question isn't about cancer any
more. It's mouse mammary tissue, the symbol is spelled `Brca1` because mouse
nomenclature capitalizes differently, and nothing in the answer will mention a
tumor. If that trade is unacceptable to you, the repair is a different dataset,
which is Chapter 23. The repair is never a vaguer question.

### Mouse studies do not translate

That's an opinion, and a common one. "Are mouse genes different from human
genes?" is the first rewrite, and it's worse than it looks. All of them?
Different how?

"How similar is mouse *BRCA1* to human *BRCA1*?" gets you a measurement with no
comparison. A percentage on its own is unreadable. Whether 73 percent identity
counts as close depends entirely on what you set beside it.

So the answerable version brings its own yardsticks. Over the coding sequences,
does human-to-mouse identity sit nearer human-to-chimpanzee or nearer
human-to-chicken? I'd be wrong if mouse came out nearer chimpanzee. You ran
that alignment in Chapter 19. Human to chimpanzee came back 99.28 percent,
human to mouse 73.18, human to chicken 49.25. Take the gaps:
99.28 − 73.18 = 26.10, and 73.18 − 49.25 = 23.93. Mouse lands in the middle, a
little closer to the chicken end.

And here's the limit, which belongs to the question rather than to the answer:
that's one gene. It settles nothing about mouse models in general, and a
sentence claiming otherwise would be a bigger claim with the same evidence
under it.

### Antibiotic resistance

"Which bacteria are resistant to antibiotics?" is a lookup. Somebody wrote that
list already and copying it isn't analysis.

"Does carrying a resistance gene make a strain resistant?" implies a comparison
without naming one, and names no measurement at all.

Answerable: take a collection of bacterial isolates where somebody recorded
which ones grew on the drug. Is a named resistance gene present in the
resistant isolates and absent from the susceptible ones? The comparison is
resistant against susceptible, counted both ways. The measurement is one yes or
no per isolate. I'd be wrong if the gene turns up at similar rates in both
piles.

You don't have that file yet, and notice what decides whether you ever will.
The sequences are in the archives by the thousand. What's scarce is a record of
which isolates grew on the drug and which didn't. A genome collection carrying
no resistance labels can't answer this, however many genomes it holds. Chapter
23 is where you check that before you spend an evening on it.

## One that does not narrow

Plenty of people arrive at this field carrying a version of this question.
"Cancer runs in my family and I want to know whether we carry something."

Run it through the three parts and watch it fail on the first one. The
comparison would be your relatives against some group of people without the
disease. The measurement would be the sequence of *BRCA1* in named individuals.
That's where it stops. Nothing in a public archive is labeled with your aunt's
name, and if it were you shouldn't be able to find her in it. Human deposits
are de-identified before they go up, and that property is what makes them
public.

So abandon it. Not narrow it, not park it until you know more: this book can't
get you there and neither can public data. Testing named people for inherited
cancer risk is a clinical service and it runs down a different road.

One warning before you move on, because the near miss costs more than the
failure. You can ask which *BRCA1* variants have been classified as pathogenic
and by whom. That question is answerable, and it's the one you'll drift toward,
and it tells you nothing about your family. Answering the neighboring question
and reporting it as the original is the most expensive mistake in this chapter.

The rule generalizes past this case: if the answer would be about one named
person, public data can't produce it. The same holds for any measurement nobody
has made yet: an experiment that hasn't been run isn't sitting in an archive,
however good the question is.

## Three weeks beats three sentences

Give a first project three weeks of the three hours a week Chapter 1 asked you
for. Three times three is nine hours in total, and Exercise 23.1 spends one of
them before you compute anything.

Nine hours is why the questions above are small. Each one ends in an object you
can name before you start. For the *Brca1* question that object is two group
means and a plot with 12 points on it. Write that end state down first. If you
can't describe what you'll be holding when you're done, the scope isn't set,
and no amount of work will set it.

Nine hours into a question you can state in three sentences and can't finish,
you're holding a folder of half-run notebooks and no number. The small question
pays out. The large one describes well at parties.

One more thing, and it cuts against instinct. A question somebody has already
answered makes a better first project than an open one, because their answer is
the only thing you can check yours against. That's why Chapter 1 promised you a
reproduced figure rather than a discovery. Asking a dataset something its own
authors never asked is allowed too. The team who generated GSE60450 was chasing
*Mcl1*, and *Brca1* sits in their file because the sequencing covered every
gene. What you give up there is the check.

## Exercises

::: {.exercise num="22.1" time="30 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Rewrite a question you actually care about until all three parts are on the
page.
:::
::: {.produce}
Four lines: the statement you started from, two versions in between, and a
final question. The final one carries two group names with a sample count
beside each, one measurement with its unit, and a sentence beginning "I would
be wrong if".
:::
::: {.check}
Your final line should carry at least two numbers, and they should be the sizes
of the two groups. No numbers means you named categories rather than samples,
and a category can't be counted. Then cover the line and write down what kind
of file you'd open first and which column you'd read out of it. If you can't
name a column, the measurement isn't named either.
:::

::: {.answerspace lines="6"}
:::
:::

::: {.exercise num="22.2" time="20 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Move each statement below one step less vague, then say which part is still
missing.
:::
::: {.given}
1. Sleep affects the immune system.
2. Some tumors come back after treatment and some don't.
3. Gut bacteria have something to do with obesity.
:::
::: {.produce}
Three rewritten lines, and beside each one the name of the part that's still
absent: the comparison, the measurement, or the direction you could be wrong
about.
:::
::: {.check}
At least one of your three should still be missing a part after one step. One
step is rarely enough, and three that all came out answerable means you jumped
the middle version. Look at your measurements too. If one of them reads
"activity" or "level", you've named a subject where a number goes.
:::

::: {.answerspace lines="6"}
:::
:::

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="Your question still contains the words is involved in"}
"Involved" is a relationship, and no file has a column for it. Say what you'd
count instead. If the honest answer is that you don't know what you'd count,
the missing part is the measurement, and Chapter 20 is where the countable
things live.
:::

::: {.errfix err="You have two named groups and no dataset containing both of them"}
Change the groups, not the shape of the question. A vaguer question is harder
to check and it fails on the same file anyway. Chapter 23 shows you which
groupings somebody has already deposited.
:::

::: {.errfix err="You cannot finish the sentence I would be wrong if"}
The question can only come out one way, so it'll come out that way on any
input. The usual culprit is the word "differ" with no threshold under it. Pick
the number that would change your mind and write it down before the run.
:::

::: {.errfix err="You have four questions and no way to choose between them"}
Pick the one whose data you can already open. Against a budget of nine hours, a
middling question you finish beats a good one you abandon in week two.
:::
:::

::: {.checkpoint}
- Name the two groups in your question and how many samples sit on each side
- Finish the sentence "I would be wrong if" for a question you care about
- Rewrite a topic into a question and say which part you added at each step
- Say why a question about one named person can't be answered from a public
  archive
- Check a question against nine hours of work and cut it until it fits
:::
